narrative:
The model estimated a 77% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That means, among applicants with a similar profile, roughly three out of four were predicted to fail; because law school admission here treats that risk as too high, your application was denied.

The decision was driven mainly by your class standing. Your third-year class-rank decile was the single strongest factor pushing toward failure, and your first-year class-rank decile was second; both placed you in the lowest decile, well below the accepted-student averages near the middle of the class. Those early and later academic rankings weighed heavily against admission. Your undergraduate GPA was the third most important factor. It was below the accepted-student average, but in the model’s overall balance it leaned slightly toward passing rather than failure; it was not enough to offset the class-rank signals.

To move forward, ask admissions whether you can appeal or receive feedback, and whether a retake or additional coursework would be considered. If you reapply, address the low class-rank pattern directly in an addendum, show any improvement or circumstances, and strengthen your LSAT preparation if time allows. A candid conversation with an admissions advisor and a realistic bar-readiness plan would help you present a stronger case next time.
